name: extension-interface
intent: Give a component a small, stable base interface plus one query operation, so clients can ask at runtime for exactly the extra capability they need and must treat absence as a normal empty answer - never an exception - allowing new or client-specific interfaces to be added without editing the component or breaking the clients that never ask for them.
problem: Different clients need different views of the same component: a spell checker wants word-level access to documents, an outline view wants headings, a properties view wants editable fields. Putting all of those operations on the component's base interface bloats it - every implementor must supply stubs it cannot honour, classes implementing the interface break whenever a client-specific operation is added, and a change to one client's part of the contract forces a rebuild or a re-release of all of them. Coupling clients to concrete component types instead is worse: it defeats substitutability and multiplies the combinations that single inheritance cannot express.
context: Component and framework designs where the component's clients are not all known when it is designed and shipped: plug-in hosts, IDEs and editors, compound-document and entity/component toolkits, product lines whose third parties add interfaces to a base type years after it shipped, and distributed-object middleware with versioned interfaces. The same shape appears at a smaller scale inside one codebase whenever a collaborator may or may not support an optional capability (flush, seek, dispose) that most callers never need. The pattern assumes the base interface is a stable contract owned by someone else - or by an earlier release - and that a missing extension is a normal, non-exceptional outcome.
benefits: Base interfaces stay small and stable: a client-specific interface is declared separately and asked for at run time, so the component's own type never gains members it cannot honour.

Existing clients and implementors are untouched - adding an extension does not recompile or re-release code that never asks for it, which is the pattern's main reason in shipped-framework and product-line settings.

Clients can be developed and shipped independently of the component and of each other, and one component can present many roles without a sub-class per combination (a limit that single inheritance cannot express).
Extensions can be supplied for classes you do not own: because the extension object need not be the subject, an adapter or factory can hand a compatible interface to a foreign type.
Capability is opt-in and checkable: callers probe once and choose a fallback, and the extension object is a natural unit of state, caching and lifetime.
tradeoffs: The lookup discards static guarantees: a missing extension is a null path the compiler cannot see, and string- or symbol-keyed identifiers turn typos and collisions into run-time failures.

A capability that is optional in the signature can still be required in practice: a caller that cannot proceed without it (hijacking a connection, flushing a response) converts the empty answer into a run-time error path, so 'optional' hides a static requirement.

Indirection costs: dynamic casts per query, adapter objects allocated per subject (or a per-object extension table), and reflection-based structural probes (Python protocol checks, Scala's reflective Selectable) that are markedly slower than a direct call.

Hidden contracts: the set of extensions an object supports is invisible to IDEs, rename refactorings and call-graph tools, so unused extensions rot and the supported set has to be documented as folklore or registry metadata.

Lifecycle and concurrency: cached extensions attach to subjects, adapter factories and registries are shared state, and per-object extension (extend, defineProperty, singleton classes) races when two threads grow the same object.

Design gravity: once a lookup exists it tends to absorb everything, producing designs where nothing is known statically - the extension mechanism then re-implements what a required interface parameter, a generic bound or a versioned interface would have stated plainly.

Version skew between host and extension: when the host ships a new extension interface version that existing extensions have not implemented, the extension silently fails to expose the capability, and the caller falls through to a degraded path with no warning.

Diamond dependency problem in plugin systems: two plugins may declare a dependency on different versions of the same extension interface, causing ClassCastException or type mismatches at runtime when the host loads both.

Lifecycle mismatch: an extension object outlives or outlasts its subject (or vice versa) — the adapter holds a reference that prevents GC, or the subject is destroyed while the extension still holds a callback into it.

Classloader isolation failures in JVM plugin systems: extensions loaded by separate classloaders cannot cast to interfaces loaded by the host classloader even when the interface is structurally identical, producing cryptic ClassCastException at the extension boundary.
Silent partial implementation: an extension claims to implement a capability but only partially honours the contract, causing subtle failures at call sites that assumed complete support.

participants.responsibility: The component that exposes the base interface and the (usually single) query operation for extensions; it decides which extensions it supports and may create, cache or adapt them on demand.
The client-specific contract that a client asks for; it is small and independent of the base interface, so it can be added or versioned without touching the Subject.
The object that implements an Extension Interface for a specific Subject (or adapts another object to it); it usually knows its owner and shares - or is released with - its lifetime.
Asks the Subject for an extension, treats absence as a normal case, and never depends on the extension being present; it uses the returned object and otherwise falls back.
The type object, symbol, GUID or name that identifies an extension and makes the query unambiguous; it is the lookup key, so its uniqueness discipline decides whether collisions are possible.
Optional: supplies extensions for subjects that do not provide them, keyed by subject type - needed when extensions must be attached to types that cannot be edited (external extensions).

use_cases: IDE and plug-in hosts adapting foreign model objects to views, editors and property sheets — the Eclipse realization has three documented steps: does the object implement the type, then IAdaptable.getAdapter, then the AdapterManager over registered adapter factories.

Compound-document and component toolkits where one component must serve unrelated clients (a spell checker wants word access, an outline wants headings) without every component implementing the union of those interfaces.
Entity/component systems and game toolkits attaching optional capabilities to entities and querying them per entity instead of widening the base Entity type for every subsystem.

Framework and product-line API evolution: a shipped base type gains interfaces years later (the 'I*2 extension interface' style), including distributed-object middleware whose interface negotiation (COM QueryInterface, CORBA narrowing) must not break older clients.

Standard-library and middleware boundaries that need a cheap capability probe on a value they did not create — Go's io.WriterTo / io.ReaderFrom probes, Python's isinstance(x, Iterable), a C# object that may or may not be IFormattable.

Java SPI (java.util.ServiceLoader): runtime discovery of service providers via META-INF/services/ lookup, enabling JDBC drivers, JAXP parsers, and SLF4J bindings to be plugged into a core API without the core knowing implementations at compile time.

Browser extension systems (Chrome, Firefox, VS Code): the host exposes a restricted API surface; extensions register capability manifests and receive API objects through a query/discovery mechanism — the pattern applied at the process boundary.

Build-tool plugin architectures (Webpack loaders, Babel plugins, ESLint configs): the tool discovers plugins via glob or config, loads them dynamically, and queries each for the specific compilation-pass interface it supports — extensions are discovered and invoked, not directly called.

Rust std::any::Any as the language-level realization: a &dyn Any answers downcast_ref::<T>() with Some(&T) or None - absence is the Option's normal case - and TypeId serves as the type-object extension identifier the pattern's uniqueness discipline recommends.

GObject/GTK's GType system: C types declare GInterfaces queried at runtime (g_type_interface_peek), and g_type_add_interface_dynamic with G_IMPLEMENT_INTERFACE_DYNAMIC lets a loaded module attach an interface to an already-shipped type - external extensions supplied for types whose code cannot be edited.

Firefox/Gecko components: every XPCOM object inherits nsISupports, whose QueryInterface(iid) returns the requested interface pointer or NS_ERROR_NO_INTERFACE, carrying the whole Firefox component ecosystem on the COM IUnknown discipline (ABI-compatible with IUnknown on Win32).
avoid_when: The extension set is known and closed at design time: put the operations on the interface (or on a composed interface) and let the compiler check them.
You own the type and it has not shipped yet: add the members or split the type - a versioned interface reads better than a lookup.

The capability is required by the caller's work: pass it in (constructor, parameter, generic bound) instead of probing - an optional interface that is always required is a static contract hidden behind a run-time check.
Only one or two concrete clients exist: a wrapper or adapter class chosen at the call site is simpler and statically visible.
The hot path can resolve the capability once: probe at wiring time and cache the answer (or inject the extension) instead of casting per call.
anti_patterns: Fat interface growth: adding each client's operations to the base interface, with empty implementations for components that cannot honour them - exactly the bloat the pattern exists to prevent.
Lookup without a uniqueness or ownership discipline: string keys scattered across modules, so collisions and typos surface as silent 'not supported' answers at run time.
Treating an always-required capability as optional, so every call site re-implements the same failure branch instead of making it a parameter.
Creating extension or adapter objects per query (or per call): allocation churn and cache misses where a per-subject cached instance was intended.
Using a system extension point as a supported API - publishing internal roles as public interfaces, then having to keep every discovered implementation working forever.
Probing with reflection or dynamic casts in hot loops because a lookup exists, instead of declaring the capability statically.
Publishing internal extension points as public API: exposing a private role as a discoverable extension and then being forced to maintain every discovered implementation forever.
Probing by dynamic cast or reflection in a hot loop — resolve once at wiring time and cache the result instead of casting per call.
design_principles: Interface segregation: several small client-specific interfaces instead of one interface that tries to be every view of the abstraction.
Open/closed principle: the component is closed for modification but open for extension through new extension interfaces.
Composition over inheritance: capabilities are composed onto an object (each extension a separate collaborator) rather than encoded as subclasses, which also escapes single-inheritance limits.
Dependency inversion / program to an interface: clients depend on the extension interface, never on the concrete component or extension type.
Substitutability with a total query: an unsupported extension must leave the component fully usable through the base interface, and absence must be an ordinary value rather than an exception.
best_practices: Make the probe total: return null/nil/None/false for an unsupported extension and forbid exceptions, so the caller can skip the component without a special case.

Identify extensions by a type object (Class<T>, typeid/type_index, TypeId, Protocol, symbol, interface IID) instead of a bare string; where strings are unavoidable keep one registry that enforces uniqueness and namespace them.
Let the extension be an adapter over the subject rather than the subject itself, so extensions work for types you cannot edit; the adapter should implement only the extension interface.
Own and cache per-subject extension objects: create on first query, release with the subject, and document who frees the extension (the pattern text's internal-versus-external extension distinction).
Keep every extension interface versioned and additive; never edit a shipped extension interface - add a successor and let clients probe for both.
Publish the supported extensions next to the type or its provider (the getAdapterList discipline) and test both branches, supported and unsupported, because the compiler will not.
Resolve capabilities once at wiring time (constructor injection, generics, required parameters) wherever the capability set is not genuinely dynamic.

Version interfaces additively: never modify a shipped extension interface — add a v2 interface and let clients opt into it, preserving backward compatibility for old clients that probe only the original.

Implement a stable, documented discovery order (Eclipse's three-step lookup: direct implements → IAdaptable.getAdapter → AdapterManager) so extension providers can predict which adapter factory wins when multiple apply.

Treat extension lifecycle as first-class: extensions activated with the subject must be deactivated with it; use reference counting or weak references to avoid preventing garbage collection of the subject.
In multi-bundle or plugin systems (OSGi, VS Code), enforce capability boundaries: run extensions in isolated processes or classloaders so a buggy or malicious extension cannot corrupt host state.

Document the complete set of supported extension identifiers in machine-readable form (extension manifest, adapter registry) so tooling can validate the set statically and discoverability tools can enumerate it.
sources: Erich Gamma, 'Extension Object', in: Pattern Languages of Program Design 3 (Martin, Riehle, Buschmann, eds.), Addison-Wesley, 1998 — a Subject declares a query; an Extension that supports itself; GetExtension returns nil when the subject does not support the requested interface, and the Extension Interface variant is what clients ask for (pattern text: https://ecs.syr.edu/faculty/fawcett/Handouts/CSE776/PatternPDFs/ExtensionObject.pdf).
https://ecs.syr.edu/faculty/fawcett/Handouts/CSE776/PatternPDFs/ExtensionObject.pdf

https://www.eclipse.org/articles/Article-Adapters/ — the Eclipse adapter framework's three-step lookup: direct implements check, then IAdaptable.getAdapter, then AdapterManager over registered adapter factories.
https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/design-guidelines/interface — 'DO NOT add members to an interface that has previously shipped'; create a new interface instead.
https://blog.merovius.de/posts/2017-07-30-the-trouble-with-optional-interfaces/ — optional interfaces hide static type information and break when interfaces are wrapped.

Bäumer, Riehle, Siberski, Wulf, 'Role Object', Pattern Languages of Program Design 4 (PLOPD4), Chapter 2, pp. 15–32, Addison-Wesley — the canonical Role Object pattern, which extends objects via transient, dynamically attachable/detachable roles rather than static capability queries; differs from Extension Interface in that roles are relationships with lifecycle management (add/remove) whereas extensions are queried capabilities (https://riehle.org/computer-science/research/2000/plopd-4.pdf).
https://riehle.org/computer-science/research/2000/plopd-4.pdf — Role Object pattern full paper.

https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/java/util/ServiceLoader.html — Java's java.util.ServiceLoader is the language-level realization of the Service Provider Interface (SPI) pattern, a discovery-only variant of Extension Interface where the host locates providers via META-INF/services/ without per-subject query semantics (contrast with Eclipse's per-object getAdapter).

https://docs.oracle.com/javase/tutorial/ext/basics/spi.html — Java SPI tutorial: Service (interface), ServiceProvider (implementation), ServiceLoader (runtime discovery); covers limitations: no runtime change notification, no ordering guarantees, no lifecycle management beyond loading.

https://docs.osgi.org/specification/osgi.core/8.0.0/framework.service.html — OSGi Core 8 Service Layer: ServicePermission-based access control, service lifecycle (register/get/unregister), happens-before visibility guarantees, class-loader isolation to prevent ClassCastException across bundles; key pitfall: lifecycle mismatch between bundle and service.

https://docs.osgi.org/specification/osgi.core/8.0.0/framework.lifecycle.html — OSGi Core 8 Lifecycle Layer: bundle start/stop resource allocation, deferred activation ordering, cleanup requirements; resources allocated in start() must be freed in stop() to avoid leaks.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/com/queryinterface--navigating-in-an-object — COM IUnknown::QueryInterface as the original binary C++ realization: three rules (object identity, static interface set, symmetric cross-interface queries); returns S_OK + pointer or null/error; absence is normal and caller must handle gracefully.

https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/com/rules-for-implementing-queryinterface — COM QueryInterface rules: identity, static interface surface, symmetric interface traversal; failure to adhere causes QI to silently return wrong pointers.

https://code.visualstudio.com/api/advanced-topics/extension-host — VS Code Extension Host architecture: runs extensions in isolated Node.js/browser/remote processes, lazy activation via extensionKind manifest (ui vs workspace preference), lifecycle managed via onDidActivateExtension / onDidDeactivateExtension events; extensions are sandboxed from the main process.

https://pkg.go.dev/io@go1.26.5 — Go io.WriterTo interface as a stdlib Extension Interface probe: type WriterTo interface { WriteTo(w Writer) (n int64, err error) }; io.Copy detects it via type assertion and bypasses the read/write loop; absence is normal (falls back to default copy) — the canonical Go idiom for optional-capability discovery (https://avtok.com/2014/11/05/interface-upgrades.html).

https://avtok.com/2014/11/05/interface-upgrades.html — Go interface upgrades: io.WriterTo and io.ReaderFrom as optional optimization interfaces; comma-ok idiom for safe type assertions; performance tradeoffs of bypassing the read/write loop.

Linda Rising, Patterns Almanac (https://smallmemory.charlesweir.com/almanac/almanac/Gamma98.html) — Extension Object parallels Decorator and Visitor; also covers Role Object (https://smallmemory.charlesweir.com/almanac/almanac/BaumerEtc99.html) distinction: Role Object is for transient client-specific views, Extension Object for stable capability discovery.

https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.5555/273448.273455 — ACM bibliographic entry for Erich Gamma's 'Extension Object', Pattern Languages of Program Design 3: the canonical record of the pattern this entry generalises as Extension Interface.

https://doc.rust-lang.org/stable/std/any/trait.Any.html — Rust std::any::Any: downcast_ref::<T>() returns Option<&T>, None when the concrete type differs; TypeId is the type-object extension identifier and Any is dyn-compatible, so trait objects support the probe.

https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/any/ — std::any module: documents the container-vs-payload trap where type_id() on a Box<dyn Any> yields the container's TypeId, requiring coercion to &dyn Any to reach the payload's identity.

https://docs.gtk.org/gobject/func.type_add_interface_dynamic.html — GObject g_type_add_interface_dynamic: attaches an interface to an existing instantiable type at run time via a GTypePlugin — the external-extension case where the type's own code cannot be edited.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mozilla-firefox/firefox/main/xpcom/base/nsISupports.idl — Firefox's nsISupports IDL: QueryInterface(iid) runtime interface discovery plus AddRef/Release lifetime, the base interface every XPCOM/Gecko component implements.

https://dzfrias.dev/blog/downcasting-invalidates-abstraction/ — criticism: probing an abstraction for subtypes invalidates the abstraction and undermines static type safety (failed casts become run-time panics); prefer tagged unions or static dispatch unless the probe is genuinely dynamic.

https://www.yegor256.com/2015-04-02/class-casting-is-anti-pattern.html — criticism: type-checking clients discriminate against objects that merely fulfil the contract, creating hidden coupling a polymorphic design would not have.

https://kotlinlang.org/api/core/kotlin-stdlib/kotlin.coroutines/-abstract-coroutine-context-key/ — Kotlin polymorphic CoroutineContext keys deprecated since 2.4 as error-prone; official guidance is to query the base key and cast explicitly — evidence that over-flexible extension identifiers fail in practice.

related_patterns_notes.extension-object: GoF Extension Object (Gamma, PLOPD3) is the canonical name; 'Extension Interface' is the more general framing. Extension Object is subject-centric: the subject returns extension objects. Role Object (Bäumer, PLOPD4) is the closely related pattern that models transient roles with add/remove lifecycle, whereas Extension Interface models static capability queries.
related_patterns_notes.role-object: Bäumer et al. PLOPD4: roles are transient, dynamically attachable/detachable relationships between a core object and a client context. Extension Interface is for stable, queried capabilities. Role Object adds lifecycle management (add/remove roles at runtime) which Extension Interface does not prescribe. Role Object often builds on Decorator and Product Trader.
related_patterns_notes.adapter: Adapter converts an incompatible interface into one a client expects. Extension Interface often uses an adapter internally (the Concrete Extension IS an adapter), but Extension Interface is primarily a capability discovery mechanism (what can this object do?) whereas Adapter is a structural conversion (how do I make this object look like X?).
related_patterns_notes.dynamic-proxy: Dynamic Proxy (Java java.lang.reflect.Proxy, .NET System.Reflection.Emit) generates a proxy class at runtime that implements a given interface and delegates to an InvocationHandler. Used to implement Extension Interface clients that need to intercept or lazy-load extension behaviour without a concrete class per interface.
related_patterns_notes.plugin: Plugin is a deployment and packaging pattern (a separately deployable module with a manifest). Extension Interface is the structural mechanism that plugins use to expose capabilities to the host. A plugin without an extension query mechanism is just a library; the extension interface is what makes it a plugin.
related_patterns_notes.visitor: Visitor adds operations to an object hierarchy without modifying the hierarchy itself — the visitor traverses and applies an operation. Extension Interface adds views of a single object without modifying it. Both escape the static type hierarchy but for different purposes: traversal+operation vs. capability discovery.
related_patterns_notes.abstract-document: Abstract Document (from DDD / java-design-patterns) uses Extension Object internally to handle dynamic properties: a Document node stores a map of property name → value, and typed getters are implemented via extension interface lookups on the node. The pattern applies Extension Interface as its implementation technique.
related_patterns_notes.strategy: Strategy encapsulates a replaceable algorithm and binds it at construction/wiring time with a compile-time-known interface. Extension Interface discovers capabilities at runtime that the subject may or may not support. Strategy is about pluggable behaviour the caller chooses; Extension Interface is about capability discovery the subject offers.
related_patterns_notes.decorator: Decorator wraps a subject and adds behaviour dynamically, with the client choosing to use the decorated view. Extension Interface returns a separate object (an adapter over the subject) that the client also chooses to use. Both allow behaviour to be added without modifying the subject, but Decorator wraps and modifies the call path, while Extension Interface returns a side-channel object.
